Question: What is Singapore doing to fight scams?
Answer:
Singapore is taking a multi-faceted, cross-agency approach to fight scams, focusing on operational improvements, stronger countermeasures, and technology adoption. Key actions include:

- Establishing and empowering specialized command and collaboration:
  - Anti-Scam Command (ASCom) was set up in 2022. Bank staff and government officers work together with the Singapore Police Force (SPF) to detect, disrupt, and prevent scams. In 2023, ASCom achieved:
    - Prevention of S$44 million in potential scam losses
    - Freezing over 19,600 tainted bank accounts
    - Recovery of more than S$100 million
  (Source: smartnation2-report.pdf, pages 35–36)

- Enhancing operational responses:
  - Improving the detection of unfolding scams, tracing of proceeds, and preventing scammers from communicating with victims and moving funds.
  - Collaboration among SPF, ASCoM, banks, and government offices to fight scams and recover funds (e.g., S$100 million recovered as noted in the Trust/Online Safety narrative). (Source: smartnation2-report.pdf, pages 37)

- Implementing strong countermeasures:
  - Government-wide ID and messaging safety measures:
    - Since July 2024, all government agencies send SMS from a single sender ID to distinguish authentic government SMS from fraudulent ones.
    - Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) established the Singapore SMS Sender ID Registry; mandatory registration for organizations using SMS sender IDs; associated reduction in scam cases involving SMSs by around 70%.
  - Telcos block calls from known scam numbers and robocalls; subscribers can opt to block international calls/SMS.
  - Banks implement emergency “kill switches” to suspend compromised accounts and prevent funds transfer.
  (Source: smartnation2-report.pdf, pages 36–37)

- Outcomes and figures:
  - Notable figures cited include recovery of over S$100 million, S$44 million prevented in 2023, 19,600 tainted accounts frozen, and about a 70% reduction in SMS-based scam cases due to sender ID measures. (Source: smartnation2-report.pdf, pages 36–37)
